title: Practical ambient-temperature superconducting conductors

concept.text: The innovation would be a reproducible material and manufacturing process for conductors that remain superconducting at ordinary temperatures and ambient pressure while carrying useful electrical currents. Superconductivity would need complementary electrical and magnetic verification, including zero resistance and magnetic-field expulsion. A transition observed in a laboratory sample would be an initial scientific achievement; the intended capability also requires a usable conductor.

Engineering synthesis: Practical conductors would need adequate current density, tolerance of magnetic fields, mechanical durability, stable electrical connections, and consistent manufacture. Their specified operating range would have to accommodate the temperatures encountered in their intended applications. Ambient-pressure operation and ambient-temperature operation are separate requirements: a material can satisfy the first while still requiring substantial cooling.

The supplied research illustrates that distinction. Deng and colleagues reported superconducting transition onsets up to 151 K at ambient pressure in pressure-quenched HgBa₂Ca₂Cu₃O₈+δ, commonly called Hg-1223. This is well below ordinary room temperature, and the retained state has thermal and temporal stability limitations. It provides a relevant laboratory advance without demonstrating the practical capability described here.

significance.text: Conditional engineering consequence: An affordable conductor that carried large currents without DC resistance at ordinary temperatures could eliminate refrigeration needed specifically to keep that conductor superconducting. With sufficient field tolerance, durability, and manufacturability, this could substantially change the design and accessibility of superconducting magnets and low-loss electrical links. Removing this refrigeration requirement would not establish that every component of the surrounding equipment could operate without cooling.

The supplied paper motivates higher-temperature superconductivity through potential energy and controlled-fusion applications, but it does not demonstrate deployment economics or quantify benefits for those applications. Grid-wide energy savings, cheaper medical imaging, and improved fusion equipment remain conditional possibilities whose realization would depend on equipment design, materials costs, manufacturing, and other technical advances.

Engineering synthesis: Zero DC resistance in the superconducting material would not make an entire installation lossless. AC losses, resistive losses in joints where present, and other system losses would still require management. Nor does removing operating refrigeration alone establish cost competitiveness or explain all present limits on superconducting deployment. The revolutionary possibility is a major relaxation of operating constraints, with the resulting value determined application by application.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability in this record is reproducible superconductivity across a useful ordinary-temperature range at ambient pressure, retained in a stable material. The supplied Hg-1223 report reaches substantially colder temperatures and explicitly identifies thermal and temporal stability as obstacles to characterization and application. It therefore grounds an important part of the remaining gap, without establishing the complete state of the field through November 2026.

Engineering synthesis: A successful material discovery would also need to preserve superconductivity at useful current densities and in the magnetic fields generated by, or applied to, the equipment. These properties must coexist in the manufactured conductor. A high transition temperature by itself would not establish that a cable could transmit its rated current or that a magnet could operate at its required field.

Engineering synthesis: Manufacturing would have to reproduce the required material state consistently and preserve it through conductor fabrication, handling, mechanical loading, and service. Connections would need stable, measured electrical and mechanical performance. Long-term degradation, operating margins, production yield, and cost would need characterization. These are practical requirements proposed for this innovation; the supplied paper does not demonstrate them or prescribe a complete engineering checklist.

current_state.text: In the paper dated 9 March 2026, “Ambient-pressure 151-K superconductivity in HgBa₂Ca₂Cu₃O₈+δ via pressure quench,” Liangzi Deng and colleagues reported retaining enhanced superconducting behavior at ambient pressure after a pressure-quench procedure. The main text reports transition temperatures ranging from 139 K to 151 K and specifies that these are transition onset values. The maximum reported onset should therefore not be described as a demonstrated zero-resistance operating temperature of 151 K, much less as room-temperature operation.

The authors reported that the metastable superconducting phase remained stable for at least three days when kept in liquid nitrogen at 77 K. They also described degradation above 200 K and degradation following room-temperature cycling. These observations establish limited stability under specified laboratory handling conditions; they do not establish a practical service lifetime. Ambient pressure describes the retained state, while its preparation still involved pressure quenching.

This account preserves the authors’ reported result rather than treating it as independent certification. According to the supplied review, the retained artifact contained the full main article text, but the figure images and linked supplementary appendix were not supplied for inspection. The review found the main-text descriptions sufficient for the onset-temperature and stability claims above. Those access limits leave visual and supplementary-data assessment incomplete; they are not evidence that the reported result is false.

Evidence boundary: The supplied freshness record is empty, so these inputs do not establish whether subsequent developments changed the field by 1 November 2026. The supported conclusion is that this March 2026 report does not demonstrate a practical ambient-temperature conductor. A comprehensive claim about the latest worldwide result cannot be resolved from this record.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scientific demonstration: Independent laboratories should reproduce stable samples exhibiting zero resistance and magnetic-field expulsion across a specified ordinary-temperature operating range at ambient pressure. Reporting should distinguish transition onset from the temperature range over which the required superconducting behavior is demonstrated. Preparation conditions, sample variability, and thermal and temporal stability should be documented so that replication tests the same material state and capability.
completion_criteria.label: Independent reproduction of ordinary-temperature superconductivity at ambient pressure

completion_criteria.text: Proposed engineering demonstration: Manufactured cables and magnets should meet declared application-specific requirements for current density, magnetic-field tolerance, mechanical durability, and joint performance. Tests should characterize operating margins, lifetime, degradation, and reproducibility across production batches under relevant service conditions. The supplied paper’s stability findings motivate this attention to persistence, but these proposed equipment tests and benchmarks extend beyond what it establishes.
completion_criteria.label: Manufactured cables and magnets meet declared application-specific service requirements

completion_criteria.text: Proposed adoption demonstration: Measure total system cost and performance against relevant alternatives, including manufacturing, installation, operation, maintenance, and replacement. Competitiveness in multiple applications would be an ambitious demonstration of broad practical value, rather than an established scientific standard. Temperature ranges, currents, fields, durability requirements, joint limits, and economic comparators must be specified before evaluation. Finite demonstrations would establish breadth within those tested boundaries, not universal suitability for every electrical application.
completion_criteria.label: Total system cost and performance measured against relevant alternatives

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — ELE-02, Fault-tolerant quantum computer with useful, scalable logical computation, and ELE-03, A long-distance quantum repeater network: These concepts share an interest in controlling quantum behavior in useful devices. Ambient-temperature superconducting conductors would address a material and electrical operating constraint; they would not by themselves establish protected logical computation, error correction, or reliable entanglement distribution. Any benefit to quantum hardware would require a compatible device architecture and demonstrated system performance.

Roster-based synthesis — ELE-04, Practical, energy-recovering reversible computing; ELE-08, Manufacturable ultra-low-voltage switching for general-purpose electronics; and ELE-11, Integrated photonic-electronic computing with broad system advantage: These innovations address computation and its energy or communication costs. Superconducting conductors could be complementary where electrical transport losses matter, but zero DC resistance alone does not demonstrate reversible logic, manufacturable low-voltage switching, or an overall advantage for photonic-electronic computing. Each retains its own device and system requirements.

Roster-based synthesis — ELE-05, Cheap, scalable storage for weeks to seasons of electrical supply, and ELE-09, Resilient, self-restoring power networks: Low-loss conductors could complement electrical storage and power networks, but efficient transport does not establish economical long-duration storage. Likewise, conductor performance does not provide the sensing, control, protection, and restoration capabilities needed for a self-restoring network. Storage duration and network resilience remain distinct capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis — ELE-07, Infrastructure-scale wireless electrical power delivery: Both concepts concern electrical power delivery, and superconducting components might be useful within a wireless system. A practical superconducting conductor would not itself demonstrate efficient power transfer across distance without a physical connection. Wireless delivery retains separate requirements for coupling, range, infrastructure, and system performance.

Roster-based synthesis — ELE-06, Durable, high-bandwidth two-way neural interface, and ELE-10, Broadly deployable, maintenance-free ambient-powered sensing: Reduced electrical transport losses could be a supporting benefit in suitable designs. The principal breakthroughs remain different: durable two-way communication with neural tissue for ELE-06, and sufficient ambient energy together with reliable low-maintenance sensing for ELE-10. Ambient-temperature superconductivity would not by itself establish either capability.

unresolved_issues: The empty freshness record leaves developments after the supplied March 2026 paper, including the state of the field by 1 November 2026, unresolved.
Independent replication or certification of the reported pressure-quenched Hg-1223 result is not established by the supplied inputs.
Figure images and the linked supplementary appendix were not inspected in the supplied review, leaving their contribution to evidentiary assessment unresolved.
The ordinary-temperature operating range and numerical benchmarks for current density, field tolerance, durability, joint performance, lifetime, and cost remain unspecified.
The supplied evidence does not establish scalable conductor manufacturing, practical equipment performance, or application economics for the reported material.

Competitiveness in multiple applications remains an ambitious proposed adoption criterion; the supplied evidence does not establish it as necessary for scientific completion or as a consensus threshold.

brief.title: Wires with no resistance at everyday temperatures
possible: Power cables could carry large, steady currents without electrical resistance at everyday temperatures and normal air pressure. Powerful magnets could operate without refrigeration to keep their conductors in this state.
why: Removing that refrigeration requirement could change the design and accessibility of powerful magnets and electrical links that lose little energy. Energy systems and controlled-fusion equipment could benefit.

sources.showed: They retained an enhanced superconducting state, which carries current without resistance, after rapidly releasing pressure. It still required deep cooling and degraded when warmed.
sources.quote:
Here, we achieve a record ambient-pressure T
c
of 151 K
sources.cited_for: Higher-temperature superconducting behavior can persist after the pressure used to prepare a material is removed.
sources.not_established: The result does not establish stable superconductivity at everyday temperatures or a usable conductor.

sources.who: Kapil Kumar, N. K. Karn, Yogesh Kumar and V. P. S. Awana
sources.showed: In a preprint, the researchers reported making and testing LK-99. Their sample remained highly resistive and showed no superconductivity at room temperature.
sources.quote:
The magnetization measurement unequivocally demonstrates no superconductivity being present in the 
modified Lead Apatite at room temperature.
sources.cited_for: An attempt to reproduce a claimed room-temperature superconductor found no superconductivity in the tested sample.
sources.not_established: The tested sample did not demonstrate the required electrical and magnetic behavior.

shown: Liangzi Deng and colleagues reported superconducting behavior beginning at 151 K under normal pressure, still far below room temperature. This marks where the transition began, rather than a demonstrated operating temperature with zero resistance.
The retained state lasted for days when stored in liquid nitrogen, but degraded on warming and after cycling to room temperature. Independent reproduction of this result remains to be established.
missing: Stable, independently reproduced superconductivity across a useful everyday-temperature range at normal pressure is still needed.
Manufactured conductors must carry useful currents, withstand magnetic fields and mechanical loads, and maintain reliable connections.
Consistent production, service lifetime and total equipment costs remain to be demonstrated.

milestones.label: Independent laboratories reproduce everyday-temperature superconductivity
milestones.explanation: Independent laboratories would have to reproduce stable samples with zero resistance that expel magnetic fields across a defined everyday-temperature range at normal pressure. This would establish the material’s essential capability.

milestones.label: Manufactured cables and magnets meet service requirements
milestones.explanation: Manufactured cables and magnets would have to meet declared limits for current, magnetic fields, durability, connections and lifetime across production batches. This would establish usable equipment.

milestones.label: Total cost and performance compete with alternatives
milestones.explanation: Complete systems would have to demonstrate competitive costs and performance against relevant alternatives across multiple applications. This would establish practical value within the tested uses.

uncertain: The required temperature range and thresholds for current, magnetic fields, durability, connections and cost remain unspecified.
Competitiveness across multiple applications is an ambitious adoption goal, rather than an agreed threshold for scientific success.
Zero resistance to steady current would still leave losses from changing currents, connections and other equipment to manage.

page.title: Ambient-pressure room-temperature superconducting conductors
page.definition: Manufactured wire or tape carries superconducting current at 300 K and ambient atmospheric pressure. Superconductivity means zero DC resistance and expulsion of sufficiently weak magnetic fields, called the Meissner effect.

goal.need: The DOE's 2006 workshop report estimated that refrigeration at 77 K required 10–15 W of input power per watt of heat removed, versus an ideal ratio of about 3. Operation near 300 K would avoid refrigeration needed solely to maintain superconductivity. The Hg-1223 result published on 9 March 2026 reached a resistive transition onset of 151 K, 149 K below 300 K; it did not establish zero-resistance operation at 151 K.

figures.caption: Refrigeration at 77 K in the DOE's 2006 report
figures.note: Historical report values. These ratios describe refrigeration, not total installation losses.

statements.body: US Department of Energy, Office of Basic Energy Sciences workshop
statements.quote: Grand Challenges include the discovery of a room-temperature superconductor and unraveling its mechanism.

statements.body: University of Houston and Texas Center for Superconductivity
statements.quote: ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductivity — around 300 K — remains the ultimate goal
statements.context: The university's announcement of the Hg-1223 pressure-quench result.

completion.title: Independently made wire carries >10,000 A/cm² at 300 K and ambient pressure.
completion.criterion: Independent laboratories manufacture wire or tape whose transport critical current, divided by the entire composite cross-sectional area, exceeds 10⁴ A/cm² at 300 K and ambient atmospheric pressure, under its declared service magnetic field and strain, including its current's self-field. Electrical and magnetic measurements establish superconductivity through zero DC resistance within instrumental sensitivity and low-field Meissner flux expulsion. The critical-current measurement uses a stated voltage criterion. This applies Ekin's transmission-line benchmark to a conductor specimen.
completion.set_by: Atlas operational test; no outside body was found publishing this combined acceptance criterion.
completion.basis: Searches of DOE's BES report, NIST conductor benchmarks, IEC 61788 scopes and CABLE prize rules found no combined room-temperature, ambient-pressure wire acceptance test. This Atlas test combines Houston's approximately 300 K goal with Ekin's >10⁴ A/cm² whole-wire transmission-line benchmark. It is a minimum conductor demonstration; it does not establish qualification of a complete power cable.

milestones.title: A material superconducts above 77 K at ambient pressure.
milestones.criterion: A specimen exhibits superconductivity above the 77 K liquid-nitrogen benchmark at ambient pressure, with electrical and magnetic evidence. Wu and colleagues reported zero resistance at 80 K and magnetic onset near 91 K on 2 March 1987, using 1 × 0.5 × 4 mm Y-Ba-Cu-O specimens. Deng and colleagues' five approximately 100–130 μm Hg-1223 specimens yielded 139–151 K resistive onsets on 9 March 2026; the retained phase lasted at least 3 days at 77 K but degraded above 200 K.
milestones.set_by: Field convention of exceeding liquid nitrogen's boiling temperature, explicitly identified by Wu and colleagues in their 1987 demonstration.
milestones.threshold_quote: temperature barrier of 77 K, the liquid-nitrogen boiling point

milestones.title: Independent laboratories reproduce superconductivity at 300 K and ambient pressure.
milestones.criterion: Independent laboratories reproduce synthesis and demonstrate zero DC resistance within instrumental sensitivity and low-field Meissner flux expulsion at 300 K and ambient atmospheric pressure. Kumar and colleagues' preprint, submitted on 7 August 2023 and revised on 9 August 2023, reported no room-temperature superconductivity in their synthesized LK-99 sample; this result is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Atlas operationalization of Houston's approximately 300 K goal and the conventional electrical and magnetic definition described by CERN. Searches found no published combined protocol specifying an exact temperature tolerance or replication count.

milestones.title: A wire retains a material critical current density >100,000 A/cm² at 300 K and ambient pressure.
milestones.criterion: Transport critical-current density exceeds 10⁵ A/cm² through fabricated wire or tape at 300 K and ambient atmospheric pressure, under the declared operating magnetic field and strain, including the current's self-field. The denominator is the superconducting material's area, excluding substrate and stabilizer. This applies the published material current-density convention at the entry's operating point; completion additionally requires the whole composite conductor to meet its engineering current-density benchmark.
milestones.set_by: The practical-superconductor current-density convention described by Ekin at NIST in 2004 and Yao and Ma in 2021. Their benchmark applies at the operating temperature and field; its application here is at 300 K and ambient pressure.
milestones.threshold_quote: 10^{5} A/cm^{2} at the operating temperature and magnetic field is widely accepted as the threshold for practical applications

not_found: No published conductor satisfying the combined completion test was found.
No independent replication of the pressure-quenched Hg-1223 151 K onset was found.
No common room-temperature conductor service-life, joint-resistance or production-yield threshold was found.
The full text of the 2021 room-temperature superconductivity roadmap could not be opened from IOP or the repositories tried.

results.finding: Five Hg-1223 specimens were investigated; the retained ambient-pressure resistive onset reached 151 K.
results.detail: Resistance measurements and DC magnetization provide electrical and magnetic evidence. The retrieved sample had a magnetic transition near 140 K; the retained phase degraded when heated above 200 K.

results.finding: One synthesized LK-99 sample showed no superconductivity at room temperature; magnetization was measured at 280 K.
results.detail: The sample was highly resistive and did not substantiate the original superconductivity claim. The magnetic measurement was at 280 K, not 300 K.
results.quote:
The magnetization measurements on SQUID magnetometer show that LK-99 is diamagnetic at 280K, 
and there is no sign of superconductivity in LK-99 at room temperature.

results.finding: One synthesized LK-99 sample had room-temperature resistivity greater than 10^11 Ω·cm.
results.detail: The authors synthesized three LK-99 samples and attributed the reported electrical and magnetic anomalies to Cu2S impurities. They concluded that LK-99 is not a room-temperature superconductor at ambient pressure; the required superconductivity was not demonstrated.
results.quote:
Demonstrating that the reported anomalies are associated with the impurity phase of Cu2S, we 
found that the resistivity of our sample S3 without Cu2S is huge, > 1011 Ω·cm, and that it does 
not exhibit any of the above-mentioned anomalies.
